intro.html: People differ in how they meet the world. Some greet everyone with a smile, some light up a party, and some keep to themselves. This topic gives you seven words for warmth and three for keeping apart.

Friendly: amiable, affable (easy to talk to), genial (warm), jovial (jolly), convivial (lively in company), amicable (peaceful, without quarrels) and charismatic (with a charm that draws people in). Keeping apart: aloof (cool and distant), reticent (says little) and reclusive (lives apart).

words.def: friendly and pleasant to be around
words.ex: The {amiable} bus driver greeted every rider by name.
words.ctx: Although the new neighbor looked stern in his dark suit, he turned out to be {amiable}, always ready with a wave, a joke and a helping hand.
words.etym: From Old French amiable, “friendly,” from Late Latin amicabilis, from amicus, “friend.”

mn.text: Amy smiles and says hello to everyone she passes, from the mail carrier to the dog next door. Amy is {amiable}.

labels.text: AMI-able: AMY, a FRIEND to all

scene.alt: A smiling woman named Amy waves hello to the mail carrier and a happy dog.

words.def: easy to talk to; friendly and good-natured
words.ex: The {affable} chef chatted with every diner who stopped by the kitchen window.
words.ctx: Despite his fame, the astronaut was {affable}; he answered every child’s question, posed for photos and laughed at even the silliest jokes.
words.etym: From Latin affabilis, “easy to speak to,” from affari, “to speak to”: ad (to) + fari (to speak).

mn.cue: AF-FABLE: always has a FABLE for you
mn.text: Jamal always has a funny fable for anyone who sits beside him on the park bench. He is so easy to talk to: {affable}.

scene.alt: A smiling man on a park bench tells a story to two delighted children.

words.ex: Our {genial} host met us at the door with a big smile and mugs of hot cocoa.
words.ctx: The night was cold, but the {genial} innkeeper made everyone feel at home: he lit a roaring fire, remembered every guest’s name and told cheerful stories over supper.
words.etym: From Latin genialis, “festive, cheerful,” from genius, the guardian spirit once thought to watch over each person.

mn.cue: GENIE-al: as warm as a friendly GENIE
mn.text: Sven throws open his door with a grin as wide as a genie’s: “Come in! Cocoa’s hot!” He is {genial}.

scene.alt: A big, smiling man welcomes a girl in from the cold with a mug of cocoa.

words.def: cheerful and full of good humor
words.ex: The {jovial} mail carrier whistled and joked on every porch.
words.ctx: Even after the long, rainy hike, Grandpa stayed {jovial}, singing silly songs and laughing so hard at his own jokes that everyone else started laughing too.
words.etym: From Latin jovialis, “of Jupiter”: people born under the planet Jupiter were once said to be cheerful.

mn.text: Marcus laughs so hard at his own joke that his shoulders shake, and soon the whole café is laughing with him. He is {jovial}.

cast.say: Ho ho, that’s a good one!

scene.alt: A jolly man laughs so hard he shakes, and a teen at the café table laughs along.

words.def: lively and friendly, enjoying feasts and good company
words.ex: The {convivial} picnic went on long after the sun went down.
words.ctx: The dinner was {convivial} rather than formal: neighbors passed dishes, swapped stories and laughed until the candles burned low.
words.etym: From Latin convivium, “a feast,” from con (together) + vivere (to live).

mn.text: At the block party there’s food on every table, music in the air and laughter all around, with everyone living it up together. The party is {convivial}.

scene.alt: Neighbors dance, eat and laugh together at a lively block party.

words.ex: After the game, the two teams shook hands and parted on {amicable} terms.
words.ctx: Even after they decided to close their shop, the partners stayed on {amicable} terms; they split the tools fairly and still meet for lunch every Friday.
words.etym: From Late Latin amicabilis, “friendly,” from amicus, “friend.”
words.note: Amiable describes people (an amiable host); amicable usually describes relationships and agreements (an amicable settlement).

mn.cue: A-MIC-able: share the MIC, no fight
mn.text: Maya and Rosa both want to sing, so instead of quarreling, they share the microphone and sing together. Their deal is {amicable}.

scene.alt: Two teens share one microphone on stage, singing together happily.

words.def: having a charm that draws people in
words.ex: The {charismatic} coach could fire up the whole team with a single smile.
words.ctx: The new student was not loud or flashy, yet she was {charismatic}; within a week, half the class wanted to sit with her at lunch.
words.etym: From Greek charisma, “a gift, a favor,” from charis, “grace.”

mn.text: When Tia walks into the room, everyone turns and drifts toward her, as if she were holding a magnet. She is {charismatic}.

scene.alt: A smiling woman holds up a magnet, and two children drift happily toward her.

words.def: cool and distant; not friendly or involved
words.ex: The {aloof} cat watched the party from the top of the bookshelf.
words.ctx: At the reunion, everyone hugged and chatted, but Victor stayed {aloof}, standing alone by the window and answering questions with a single word.
words.etym: From an old sailors’ word meaning “to windward,” used of steering a ship away from something; aloof people keep their distance.

mn.cue: A-LOOF: alone up on the ROOF
mn.text: While the family plays in the yard below, the cat sits alone on the roof and won’t come down. The cat is {aloof}.

scene.alt: A bored cat sits alone on a rooftop while children below call for it to come play.

words.def: not willing to say much or to share thoughts and feelings
words.ex: Usually {reticent}, Sami surprised everyone with a long, funny speech at his sister’s graduation.
words.ctx: Asked about the fire, the {reticent} witness said only “I saw smoke” and would not add a word, no matter how hard the reporters pressed.
words.etym: From Latin reticere, “to keep silent”: re (back) + tacere (to be silent), the same root as tacit.
words.note: Reticent means reluctant to speak or share, not reluctant in general. For “unwilling,” use reluctant.

mn.cue: RETI-CENT: not one CENT’s worth of words
mn.text: Ask Lin about her weekend, and you won’t get one cent’s worth of words: just a smile and a shrug. She is {reticent}.

labels.text: RETI-CENT: not a CENT of words

scene.alt: A teacher asks a shy woman to talk about herself, and she only puts a finger to her lips.

words.def: avoiding the company of other people; living alone and apart
words.ex: The {reclusive} painter rarely left her cabin in the woods.
words.ctx: The famous author was so {reclusive} that he had not given an interview in forty years; letters went unanswered, and his gate stayed locked.
words.etym: From Late Latin reclusus, “shut away,” from re- (back, away) + claudere (to shut).

mn.text: Omar lives alone in a cabin deep in the woods, with the door closed and a sign out front. He is {reclusive}.

scene.alt: A shy man hides beside his cabin deep in the forest, behind a sign that says Please Go Away.

after.cap: Seven ways to be warm, and three ways to keep apart.

after.html: Two pairs to watch. Amiable describes people (an amiable host), while amicable usually describes relationships and agreements (an amicable settlement, amicable relations). And reticent means unwilling to speak or share, not unwilling in general: you can be reticent about your feelings, but you are reluctant, not reticent, to clean your room.

opts.s: Though the brothers disagreed about who should get the car, the talk stayed {amicable}, and they agreed to take turns.
opts.why: A talk without quarreling, ending in a fair deal, is amicable.

items.q: The two bakeries reached an ______ agreement about sharing the parking lot, with no hard feelings on either side. Which word fits?
items.why: Amicable describes relationships and agreements that are friendly and free of quarrels.

items.q: True or false: reticent means unwilling to do anything at all.
items.why: False. Reticent means unwilling to speak or share thoughts. For being unwilling in general, the word is reluctant.

items.q: Convivial comes from Latin convivium, which means…
items.why: A convivium was a feast, from con (together) + vivere (to live): convivial gatherings are lively and full of company.

items.q: Which word best describes someone who lives alone far away and avoids all visitors?
items.why: Reclusive people avoid company and live apart. Aloof people may be in the room but stay cool and distant; reticent people say little.

items.q: Type the word, from the Latin name of the planet Jupiter, that means cheerful and full of good humor.
items.why: People born under Jupiter were once said to be cheerful: jovial.
